appearance-materials-brdf.problem_shape: These papers belong together because they all ask how a material can be known, drawn, changed, or designed when the visible surface is only a partial clue. A real material is not just color. It answers light differently from different directions, scatters light inside hair or feathers, hides fibers under a microscope image, folds into origami creases, carries stiffness through pores, or appears in X-ray shadows as one of several possible substances. The computer usually sees only a compressed sign of that behavior: a few measured reflection samples, a headset view of a face under unknown light, a single microscope image, sparse X-ray projections, a texture map, or a target halftone picture. The shared problem is to separate the thing itself from the conditions that revealed it. Which part is surface response, which part is lighting, which part is shape, which part is hidden internal material, and which part is mechanical behavior? The family is therefore about material identity under incomplete evidence.
appearance-materials-brdf.naive_failure: A smart beginner might store a huge table of how every material looks from every view and light direction, trace every light bounce through every hair or feather fiber, label each X-ray volume cell directly, or hand-design every fabric strand, fold, pore, and texture detail. That works only for tiny cases. Tables grow too large, dense fibers create too many light interactions, and one photo or projection cannot uniquely reveal the hidden three-dimensional structure. A beginner might also paint appearance onto a surface and hope later geometry tools preserve it. That fails when changing the surface layout moves texture evidence away from the points it describes. The deeper failure is confusion between causes: a bright cheek could be skin color or strong lighting, a dark X-ray region could be thickness or material, and a target image in a porous object could damage stiffness if treated as decoration.
appearance-materials-brdf.mathematical_principle: The recurring principle is to replace an impossible direct description with a smaller set of adjustable causes, then compare their predicted evidence with the evidence actually measured. For reflected appearance, the unknown is a rule that says how much light returns for each incoming and outgoing direction. A Gaussian process, meaning a probability rule that expects nearby measurements to behave similarly, fills in unmeasured directions while keeping uncertainty visible. For faces, fabrics, and X-ray volumes, the method guesses lighting, surface response, fiber parameters, or material probabilities, renders or projects that guess forward, and changes the guess when the synthetic evidence disagrees with the captured evidence. For feathers and hair, the enormous collection of tiny fiber events is replaced by a layered or volume-like description that keeps the average scattering behavior while preserving enough explicit detail for direct highlights. For origami and porous structures, many small creases or holes are averaged into whole-object stiffness. The math is therefore bookkeeping for hidden causes: what is stored, what is averaged, what is compared, and what must stay consistent when appearance is edited, relit, compressed, or fabricated.
appearance-materials-brdf.why_math_matters: The math matters because materials have repeated structure. Nearby reflection directions usually do not jump randomly. Neighboring fibers in a fabric follow weave patterns. Feather branches contain smaller branches. Dense hair has many individual fibers, but after several light bounces the result behaves partly like light moving through a cloudy volume. X-rays are shadows produced by known material responses along lines through space. Folded sheets and porous patterns have tiny geometry that produces a larger stiffness felt by the whole object. These regularities are why the papers can do more than memorize pictures. They exploit smoothness, repetition, averaging, and forward checking. Smoothness lets sparse BRDF measurements predict missing ones. Repetition lets a single microscope image drive a procedural fabric model instead of requiring every fiber to be drawn by hand. Averaging lets origami folds and porous holes be treated as bulk behavior. Forward checking keeps inverse tasks honest: if the recovered face, fabric, or X-ray volume cannot reproduce the captured image or projection, the explanation is wrong.
appearance-materials-brdf.paper_family: The representative papers are different branches of the same hidden-cause problem. Fast and Accurate Gaussian Process Modelling of Real-World Materials compresses measured reflection behavior into a smooth analytical rule, so a material can be queried without a giant table. EgoRelight and the facial delighting work try to separate a person or face from the light falling on it, making relighting possible from headset capture or casual video. The feather and hair scattering papers avoid tracking every fiber-to-fiber light bounce by using multiscale or volume-like descriptions while keeping visible strand detail. Fiber-level woven fabric capture starts from one microscopic image and adjusts a procedural fabric model until its rendered appearance matches the image. Discrete X-ray computed tomography treats each volume location as a probability over known materials, then checks whether the simulated projections match the measured ones. PhaseTree stores multiple material regions compactly for volumetric objects, so inside-out material boundaries remain queryable during rendering. Texture-aware remeshing carries surface color evidence through geometry changes. Origami material homogenization and mechanical cloaking ask a related design question: how can small folds or pores create desired large-scale stiffness while still producing the intended appearance?
appearance-materials-brdf.what_changed: The 2026 pattern is that material work is moving away from static surface look-up tables and toward editable, measured, or physically useful causes. The evidence emphasizes compact analytical material rules, relightable human appearance, single-image fabric capture, real-time feather appearance, faster dense hair scattering, sparse and limited-angle tomography, multiphase volumetric storage, and material designs that couple visual images with stiffness. Another change is that appearance and mechanics are no longer separate boxes. A texture-aware surface operation must preserve what the texture means, a porous halftone must still feel mechanically uniform, and origami creases must predict whole-material behavior. The family is becoming more causal: explain the appearance well enough to change, simulate, fabricate, or relight it.
appearance-materials-brdf.limits: The evidence does not show a universal material solver. Many results depend on specific inputs: measured BRDF samples, stereo headset cameras, casual face video, a single microscopic fabric image, sparse X-ray projections, known material choices, UV texture layouts, dense hair or feather assumptions, crease patterns, or porous design templates. Learned priors may fail when the face, lighting, fabric, or material lies outside their training evidence. Averaging many fibers, folds, or pores can miss rare local effects that matter visually or mechanically. Inverse methods can still confuse causes when different material, shape, and lighting explanations produce similar images. The abstracts report contributions and selected comparisons, but they do not prove reliability under all lighting, scales, capture noise, materials, fabrication limits, or dynamic motion.

character-animation-motion.problem_shape: These papers belong together because they all treat motion as something that must satisfy several audiences at once. A character should follow an artist's intent, keep body parts connected, make contacts land in the right places, and still move as if weight, balance, timing, cloth, hands, muscles, or object interactions matter. The computer may receive a text prompt, a captured sequence, a sketch, a few seconds of style examples, a body with unusual proportions, a hand view, a cloth scan, or a streamable 3D video. None of those inputs is the motion itself. They are partial evidence about how something should change over time. The shared problem is to turn that evidence into a believable sequence of states: bones, surfaces, hands, strokes, texture, volume, or object parts at one moment, then the next, without losing identity or breaking contact. The family is wider than human walking. It includes non-human characters, athletic control, piano-playing hands, exaggerated bodies, layered drawings, deforming textures, deployable cut patterns, cloth capture, and long volumetric video. They are siblings because each asks how time can be generated, transferred, compressed, or cleaned while preserving the relationships that make motion readable.
character-animation-motion.naive_failure: A smart beginner would try to copy motion directly. Put the same joint angles on a new character, interpolate drawings halfway between key frames, smooth captured hands, repeat a stored motion clip, or compress each frame as if it were unrelated to the previous one. For control, they might ask a learned policy to imitate examples and hope it survives a new environment. These ideas fail because motion is relational. A footstep only looks right if it reaches the ground at the correct time and does not slide. A hand grasp only works if fingers, object, wrist, and body agree. A style is not just a pose; it is also rhythm, exaggeration, and which body region carries the change. A drawing stroke may disappear behind another layer. A new body shape can turn a valid action into self-contact or impossible balance. Treating frames independently also creates jitter, missing details, or huge storage cost.
character-animation-motion.mathematical_principle: The recurring math idea is coordinated change through time. Each method chooses a compact description of the moving thing, measures what must stay true, and then fills in or adjusts the missing motion so those truths conflict as little as possible. What is being adjusted may be a skeleton, muscle activations, body-root motion, finger bends, cloth surface points, stroke layers, soft 3D video anchors, character proportions, or movable CAD parts. What counts as wrong depends on the paper: drifting away from a reference action, breaking contact, losing self-contact after retargeting, mismatching captured cloth, producing unstable volumetric video, asking muscles to perform an incoherent command, or failing to honor a sketch's intended joint. Several papers use learning, meaning they reuse patterns seen in examples, but the useful idea is not the label. The useful idea is that examples provide a smaller space of likely motions, while constraints keep the result tied to the current body, object, camera, or timing. Other papers split motion into pieces: posture versus timing, root motion versus body detail, coarse cloth shape versus wrinkles, or old frame content versus the change from one frame to the next. The tradeoff is freedom versus consistency: enough freedom to create or adapt motion, enough consistency that the viewer believes the moving object is the same physical thing over time.
character-animation-motion.why_math_matters: The math matters because motion has structure that a single picture cannot reveal. Bodies have parts connected by joints; hands have many small controls that must act together; muscles create motion indirectly through forces; cloth and deformable surfaces carry wrinkles from nearby frames; drawings have visible and hidden layers; volumetric video contains pieces that persist while the camera sees changing surfaces. These structures make time predictable in limited ways. If a hand is touching a piano key now, the next frame should not teleport the finger away unless the action says so. If a character has longer arms, the old motion must bend around that shape instead of simply replaying old numbers. If a motion style is learned from a few seconds, the system must separate what is a stable posture preference from what is a timing pattern, or it will copy the example too literally. Anchors, constraints, losses, policies, and decompositions are bookkeeping devices for these relationships. They tell the method which differences are allowed, which differences signal a mistake, and which details can be reused from neighboring time steps or examples.
character-animation-motion.paper_family: The representative papers are different branches of the same problem: carry intent through time without breaking the moving object's internal logic. ACT starts at the broadest level by joining rigging and animation, so an unusual character can receive both a controllable body structure and motion rather than treating setup and action as separate chores. HIL, MUSIC, and ReActor focus on control: an athletic body, muscle-driven hand, or robot must imitate examples while still surviving forces, balance, and new tasks. STyMo, DMP, skinned retargeting, MotionBricks, and autoregressive human motion generation adapt or create motion under user control, but each must protect timing, contacts, body proportions, or region-specific style. MOCHI and OmniHands repair or capture interactive motion where hands, objects, and multiple people create missing data and contact mistakes. LayerInbetween solves a 2D version of the same time problem by matching strokes across frames while reasoning about occlusion and layers. The compression and anchored volumetric-video papers preserve moving 3D content by storing changes and stable time anchors instead of treating every frame as new. Cloth capture, deforming texture, kirigami deployment, and Sketch2Arti show the physical and design side: surfaces, cuts, textures, and mechanical parts need motion parameters that obey how the object can actually bend, unfold, or articulate.
character-animation-motion.what_changed: The 2026 pattern is that motion work is becoming less tied to one body type, one capture setup, or one offline authoring pipeline. The evidence emphasizes arbitrary character shapes, few-shot style examples, text and constraint control, real-time streaming, zero-shot adaptation, interactive hands, collaborative human-object motion, and long volumetric sequences. Another change is stronger coupling between generated motion and physical or contact evidence. Several papers do not merely make a plausible sequence; they refine grasps, preserve self-contact, train against physics-aware goals, track muscles, or keep cloth coherent through capture. Learned models appear often, but they are increasingly wrapped around explicit controls, anchors, decompositions, and constraints.
character-animation-motion.limits: The evidence does not prove that these methods handle every body, motion, object, or capture condition. Many depend on training data, paired style examples, reference motions, template cloth, readable sketches, known CAD structure, camera views, marker patterns, or bodies close enough to the method's assumptions. Physical controllers can still fail when contacts, terrain, strength, or timing fall outside their experience. Retargeting and generation methods may preserve some contacts while losing others. Compression and volumetric-video methods assume enough temporal coherence to exploit previous frames. The abstracts describe contributions more than failure cases, so they do not establish behavior under severe occlusion, unusual anatomy, fast hand-object interaction, extreme cloth folding, unsupported art styles, or deployment on every real-time system.

cloth-hair-fibers.problem_shape: These papers belong together because cloth, hair, feathers, yarn, and woven fabric are all made from many thin pieces whose small behavior creates the visible whole. A hairstyle is not only a silhouette; it is thousands of strands arranged by scalp region and by local curl. Knitwear is not just a flat sheet; it is loops of yarn that stretch, bend, twist, touch, and constrain nearby loops. A feather is a shaft plus fine barbs and barbules whose shadows and sheen change with view and light. Woven fabric has microscopic fibers whose paths and optical behavior decide the final look. Cloth capture must recover wrinkles and folds even when the cloth hides itself. The shared problem is scale: the viewer cares about fine threads, but the computer cannot always store, simulate, capture, or light every fiber directly. These papers ask how to keep the important strand-level structure while making generation, planning, capture, motion, and appearance practical for scenes artists can inspect.
cloth-hair-fibers.naive_failure: A smart beginner might treat these materials as ordinary surfaces: paint a hair texture onto a head, bend a flat cloth sheet, draw a few feather lines from a photo, or use a woven color pattern instead of modeling fibers. They might also simulate every yarn or light bounce exactly and hope faster hardware is enough. Both instincts fail. Surface tricks lose the order of individual strands and loops, so edits break, rare hairstyles become muddled, feather rims look wrong, and fabric close-ups do not match real cloth. Exact detail fails for the opposite reason: yarn-level garments have millions of moving values, dense hair has too many light interactions, and fabric capture from one microscope image lacks direct depth information. The family needs structure that is finer than a painted surface but cheaper than brute force.
cloth-hair-fibers.mathematical_principle: The recurring mathematical idea is structured reduction: keep the relationships that matter and compress the rest into smaller, checkable pieces. For hair generation, the object is broken into strands, scalp regions, and coarse-to-fine strand descriptions, so the next strand can be predicted from the existing arrangement instead of invented as a cloudy texture. For knit planning, the surface is divided into territories by distance and weight, then singular points are moved until they distribute knitting difficulty more evenly and avoid unwanted helical paths. For yarn motion, a single tangled problem is split into smaller agreements: stretching, shearing, bending, twisting, and contact are handled as subproblems, then reconciled. For capture, measured image points or microscope pixels become a score of wrongness; fiber positions, lighting behavior, or cloth shape are adjusted until the predicted image or camera evidence matches while still obeying physical limits. For hair and feathers, many tiny light interactions are summarized by a compact description, with explicit fibers kept where sharp direct detail matters. The tradeoff is detail versus cost, with structure deciding what can be safely summarized accurately.
cloth-hair-fibers.why_math_matters: The math matters because these materials are organized, not random. Neighboring yarn loops share constraints. Nearby hair strands often follow a style pattern while still differing locally. A feather repeats barb and barbule structure across scales. Woven fibers follow over-under paths that a microscope image hints at but does not fully reveal. Cloth wrinkles are continuous through time even when cameras miss parts behind folds. Light inside dense hair or fur scatters many times, but its average travel through a thick bundle can be approximated if direction and density are respected. The papers exploit those facts. Splitting a hard solve works because different physical effects can be checked separately before being made to agree. Territory diagrams on a surface work because knitting singularities are placement problems over a connected sheet. Coarse-to-fine estimation works because large fiber layout narrows the search before fine optical details are tuned. Compact feather and hair models work because repeated microstructure can be regenerated procedurally instead of stored fiber by fiber.
cloth-hair-fibers.paper_family: HairGPT shows the generation branch: it treats strands as the basic words of a hairstyle and orders them by scalp region and strand hierarchy, so style control follows the way hair is groomed. Surface Power Diagrams for Knit Singularity Placement shows the planning branch: it places special knit points globally on the garment surface, using surface-distance territories and ordering constraints so denser knit graphs remain helix-free. Interactive Yarn-level Knitwear shows the motion branch: it does not abandon individual yarns, but it splits their many coupled forces and contacts into smaller stable solves that can run interactively. High-Fidelity 4D Cloth Capture shows the measurement branch: camera markers give incomplete 3D points, and a physical cloth template fills the hidden regions while keeping wrinkles coherent over time. Fiber-level Woven Fabric Capture uses a single microscope image to estimate fiber geometry and appearance through staged matching. Efficient Fur and Hair Multiple Scattering and the feather appearance model show the appearance branch: both keep visible fiber detail where needed while replacing impossible full detail with compact scattering or procedural structure. Pixel Cube is adjacent because facial hair and fine portrait detail must survive relighting over time.
cloth-hair-fibers.what_changed: The 2026 pattern is a move away from treating cloth, hair, and fibers as either flat surfaces or impossibly detailed brute-force objects. The evidence points to middle representations: strand tokens, surface territories, split yarn constraints, two-level cloth markers, microscope-driven fiber parameters, compact feather descriptions, and volume-like summaries for dense hair lighting. Another change is stronger editability and capture from weaker input. A single photo can seed a feather, a single microscope image can recover woven-fiber appearance, and hairstyle generation exposes semantic scalp controls. The family is also pushing toward interaction: yarn-level knitwear and feather rendering are framed around practical speed, not only final offline quality.
cloth-hair-fibers.limits: These outputs depend on structure being present and recognizable. HairGPT assumes hairstyles can be organized by scalp regions and strand sequences learned from examples. Knit singularity placement assumes the surface and user constraints give a meaningful knitting-time field and that helix-free ordering constraints fit the design. Yarn-level simulation still depends on the chosen physical energies, contact handling, and solver tolerances. Cloth capture needs visible markers, calibrated cameras, and a usable template when parts are hidden. Fabric capture from one microscope image relies on the procedural fabric model matching the real weave. Feather and hair lighting approximations can fail for unusual fibers, iridescence, extreme density, or lighting outside their tested assumptions. The evidence reports representative results, not complete failure maps.

computational-photography-imaging.problem_shape: These papers are about getting a useful picture when the camera does not directly see the thing the researcher wants to know. Sometimes the missing part is brightness, as in a phone camera trying to cover dark shadows and bright highlights with several raw exposures. Sometimes it is time, angle, or hidden space, as in GenPIE measuring sparse timed light paths or thermal non-line-of-sight imaging trying to infer a scene around a rough surface. Sometimes the missing part is color spectrum, wavefront shape, material response, fabric fibers, or the way an optical system will behave after software processing. The shared problem is that imaging is not just taking a photograph. It is a bargain between the world, the sensor, the lighting, and the reconstruction code. The sensor receives limited numbers: photon counts, exposure values, ray errors, microscopic pixels, or indirect heat signals. The family asks how to turn those partial measurements back into a believable scene, surface, material, force, or design decision without pretending the missing evidence was directly observed.
computational-photography-imaging.naive_failure: A smart beginner might try to make the sensor collect everything: take every exposure, sample every light direction, scan every wavelength, measure every wavefront change, or trace every possible light path. That fails because the space of possible measurements grows too fast. A scene can vary across position, direction, time, color, depth, and material, while a real device has limited pixels, limited light, limited frame time, and occlusions. The other naive answer is to fill the gaps with ordinary image cleanup: brighten dark pixels, average exposures, sharpen blur, or train a model to guess the missing view. That also fails when the numbers have physical meaning. A rough surface mixes hidden heat signals, a single-photon sensor has noisy and quantized counts, and a phone exposure can saturate. Simple cleanup can invent detail, destroy timing, or break the light behavior the measurement was meant to preserve.
computational-photography-imaging.mathematical_principle: The recurring principle is inverse measurement: first describe how the world would produce the sensor numbers, then search for a hidden cause whose predicted numbers match the real ones. In plain terms, the method builds a careful pretend camera. If a possible hidden scene, lens shape, material, exposure blend, or fabric layout were true, the pretend camera says what measurements should appear. The algorithm then adjusts the hidden answer until the predicted measurements are close to the captured measurements, while also obeying extra rules from physics or learned examples. What counts as wrong depends on the paper. GenPIE compares timed indirect light transport against sparse observations. Thermal non-line-of-sight imaging estimates mixing kernels, meaning recipes for how hidden heat or light from one place spreads into another. Adaptive optics recovers a wavefront, the shape of arriving light, from asymmetric aperture images. Lucky HDR combines bracketed raw pixels while keeping combinations convex, so the result is assembled from measured values rather than free invention. Hi-SPAD treats photon arrivals as counts whose errors shrink as more measurements accumulate. Optical design lifts a single image score into ray-level residuals, many small ray mistakes that can guide lens changes.
computational-photography-imaging.why_math_matters: The math matters because light and sensors have structure even when the image looks incomplete. Light does not arrive as arbitrary numbers. It travels along paths, bounces, spreads through rough surfaces, arrives at different times, changes with wavelength, and is clipped or counted by the sensor. Those regularities are exactly what make recovery possible. Multi-exposure phone imaging works because different raw images contain different trustworthy pixels, and a weighted blend can choose among measured evidence. Time-resolved imaging works because arrival time carries path length information: later light usually traveled differently than earlier light. Thermal hidden-scene imaging works only if the rough surface mixing can be described by repeatable kernels. Wavefront sensing works because a distorted wave creates predictable image changes when the aperture is deliberately asymmetric. Hyperspectral photon counting works because repeated photon counts reveal a spectrum statistically, not all at once. The neighboring papers use the same logic in other domains: material modeling compares predicted and measured reflection, fabric capture adjusts procedural fibers to match a microscope image, and radiation pressure design compares sampled photon forces against a faster proxy.
computational-photography-imaging.paper_family: The representative papers are siblings because each turns scarce measurements into a fuller account of what caused them. Lucky High Dynamic Range Smartphone Imaging stays closest to everyday photography: it uses several raw exposures and forms each output pixel from measured exposure values, aiming to avoid hallucinated detail. GenPIE moves from ordinary images to timed, angular light evidence, using decoupled laser and detector hardware plus a generative prior and a transient light-path check to bridge sparse observations. Thermal Non-Line-of-Sight Imaging is another hidden-cause problem: rough surfaces scramble the signal, so the method estimates how the surface mixes information before reconstructing hidden layout and relative depth. Guidestar-Free Adaptive Optics removes a special reference light and instead makes the aperture itself reveal wavefront errors. Hi-SPAD combines a scanning layout with single-photon sensors so space, time, and spectrum can be recovered under ambient light. Generalized Aberrations treats optical design as many ray-level mistakes rather than one vague image score. The other listed papers extend the same pattern: convert terrain images to height, capture fabric fibers from a microscope image, fit material reflection compactly, or make time-of-flight rendering fast enough to test sensing systems.
computational-photography-imaging.what_changed: The 2026 pattern in this family is that capture and computation are being designed together. The evidence is not just better post-processing after a normal camera image. Several papers change the measurement itself: decoupled illumination and detection, asymmetric apertures, pushbroom single-photon sensing, bracketed raw mobile capture, thermal hidden-scene sensing, and ray-level optical design. Learned models appear, but mostly as helpers constrained by measured evidence or physics: priors initialize missing 3D structure, networks estimate mixing kernels, and fast proxies answer force or material queries. The shift is toward sparse but intentional measurements, followed by reconstruction that knows how those measurements were made.
computational-photography-imaging.limits: These results depend on the measurement story being accurate. If exposure brackets are misaligned, saturated, or outside the assumed raw behavior, HDR fusion can still fail. If hidden-scene mixing through a rough surface does not match the estimated kernels, non-line-of-sight recovery weakens. If photon counts are too few, Hi-SPAD's spectrum estimates and material classification have less evidence. Adaptive optics needs aperture images that really reveal wavefront error, and optical design needs ray-level residuals that predict final processing behavior. Learned priors can fill gaps but may bias the answer toward familiar shapes or materials. The evidence reports contributions and speedups, not universal reliability across all lighting, motion, hardware, surfaces, or scenes.

fabrication-3d-printing.problem_shape: This family is about the moment when a computer design has to become a physical thing. On screen, a surface can bend freely, pass through itself by accident, use impossible layers, or ignore how stress travels. In the world, a printer nozzle has a size, a resin blurs as light and chemistry spread, fabric plies need manufacturable thickness, architectural panels must carry load, and a virtual object can feel real only if some nearby physical object can stand in for it. The shared problem is not just making a shape. It is converting intent into a build plan that respects matter. Each paper asks what must stay true during that conversion: a composite should become stiffer, a freeform surface should keep its look while lowering stress, a triangle surface should stop crossing through itself, a filament printer should follow continuous bead paths, a VR touch target should match a real object, and a holographic printer should deposit enough curing dose in the right tiny places. The family exists because fabrication exposes every hidden lie in a digital model.
fabrication-3d-printing.naive_failure: A smart beginner would first separate design from making. Draw the best-looking surface, then panelize it. Pick a strong composite layout, then cut fabric layers afterward. Slice a print into ordinary flat layers, then ask the nozzle to follow them. Remove surface crossings by pushing apart only the visibly colliding triangles. For touch in VR, print a matching prop or use visual feedback alone. For holographic printing, compute the light pattern and ignore how the resin keeps reacting after light arrives. These ideas fail because physical constraints are coupled. Changing a panel changes stress elsewhere. A fabric boundary changes stiffness across neighboring layers. A local untangle can create a larger knot. A nozzle path must preserve bead thickness, avoid collisions, and keep moving. A room object must match shape, position, and touch qualities. In resin, optics and chemistry blur together.
fabrication-3d-printing.mathematical_principle: The recurring mathematical principle is to turn fabrication into a scored agreement among many promises. A promise can be geometric: the surface should stay close to the intended form, should not pass through itself, and should be split into usable panels or layers. A promise can be mechanical: stress should be lowered, stiffness should rise, and material directions should carry force well. A promise can be machine-related: the filament bead should keep nearly constant thickness, the tool should not collide, and non-printing travel should be small. A promise can be sensory or chemical: a real object should match a virtual touch target, or a hologram should create a dose pattern that survives light bending and inhibitor diffusion. The method then adjusts the design, layer fields, paths, surface positions, hologram sequence, or object match to reduce the measured violations. This is optimization, meaning repeated score-and-adjust search, but the score is not abstract. It is a checklist of what would break in fabrication. The key tradeoff is design freedom versus physical obedience: enough freedom to improve shape, touch, stiffness, or resolution, but enough obedience that the result can actually be made or used.
fabrication-3d-printing.why_math_matters: The math matters because fabrication constraints are spread out, not isolated. Stress is global: a weak region may be caused by panel choices far away because load travels through the whole shell. Composite layers are directional: a fabric ply can be strong along one direction and weaker across another, so partial layer boundaries change how force moves between layers. Self-intersection is also global. A triangle surface, meaning a skin made of many flat patches, can be locally separated in one place yet still folded through itself as a whole. Filament printing is path-based: every point on a layer affects the next point because the nozzle must move continuously with a fixed bead profile. Holographic resin printing is coupled through light waves and chemistry: the projected phase pattern bends light, while curing and inhibitor diffusion smear the final solid. ProXeek uses the same logic in a different material setting: the physical room already contains objects, but a match is useful only when several constraints agree at once. Mathematics gives these papers a way to see long-range consequences before a machine or user exposes the mistake.
fabrication-3d-printing.paper_family: The papers are siblings because each replaces an after-the-fact repair step with a coupled making plan. Co-Optimization of Structure and Manufacturable Semi-Continuous Layers for Laminated Composites does not first choose a shape and later decide fabric plies. It adjusts structure and manufacturable partial layers together, modeling how layer boundaries change directional mechanical behavior, and reports higher stiffness than planar ply counterparts. Stress-Aware Panelization makes a similar move for architecture: instead of panelizing a freeform surface and only then checking strength, it lets stress analysis influence the surface flow while preserving design intent. Untangling Surfaces handles the prerequisite for many fabrication pipelines: the digital skin must be embedded, meaning it occupies space without crossing through itself, so the method uses both broad shape repulsion and local triangle-level penalties. AtomSlicer turns multi-axis filament printing into a path agreement problem, preserving orientation fields, near-constant layer thickness, continuous toolpaths, and collision avoidance, or reporting that the request cannot be fabricated. Single-View Holographic Volumetric 3D Printing couples wave optics with resin chemistry so the light plan pre-compensates for chemical blur. ProXeek broadens fabrication into opportunistic touch: rather than making a prop, it matches virtual interactables to real objects already in the room.
fabrication-3d-printing.what_changed: The 2026 pattern is that fabrication papers are moving from shape-first pipelines toward constraint-first pipelines. The evidence emphasizes joint design and manufacturing instead of cleanup after design is frozen. Composite layout, panel stress, surface untangling, multi-axis slicing, holographic curing, and VR haptic proxy selection all treat fabrication limits as part of the main computation. Another change is stronger honesty about feasibility. AtomSlicer preserves user or solver-defined fields and reports non-fabricability rather than quietly changing the request. The holographic printer models both optics and chemistry rather than only the projected light. ProXeek compares real room objects against touch constraints instead of assuming a custom printed replica is the best physical answer.
fabrication-3d-printing.limits: These results depend on the chosen physical models and inputs. Composite design assumes the layer field, stiffness model, and manufacturing objectives describe the real fabric plies well enough. Stress-aware panelization depends on the shell model, stress objective, and architectural shapes tested. Untangling assumes the surface representation can be moved without changing connectivity and that repulsion energies capture the relevant crossings. AtomSlicer assumes supplied orientation fields, bead profile, and machine collision checks match the printer. Holographic volumetric printing is shown on small volumes and simple structures, with simplified photochemistry. ProXeek depends on headset snapshots, annotations, language-model reasoning, and available room objects. The evidence reports selected validations, not universal guarantees across all materials, printers, rooms, scales, noise levels, or manufacturing tolerances.

faces-avatars.problem_shape: This family is about making a person, object, or surface usable when the computer only has indirect evidence. A headset sees a face and nearby lighting from awkward cameras. Several cameras see body joints from different angles. A point cloud gives scattered samples but not a clean skin. A deforming surface stretches a texture until painted detail slides or blurs. A roof outline, a material-filled volume, or a hidden warm object gives only partial clues about the shape that should exist. The shared pressure is that visual work needs a stable thing to render, edit, collide, relight, or animate, but the evidence is incomplete, noisy, or expensive to query everywhere. The papers therefore ask how to store the object in a form that can answer many questions: where the surface is, how it bends, how it moves, how light changes across it, and how much uncertainty remains. Avatars are the most human-facing case of this problem, but the same shape-and-evidence difficulty also appears in roofs, panels, hidden scenes, and deformable textures.
faces-avatars.naive_failure: A smart beginner might try to capture or store everything directly: scan every point, evaluate every possible viewing ray, keep a dense grid of inside and outside values, run one large pose fit across all people and cameras, or paint texture coordinates once and hope they keep working as the surface stretches. That fails because the real object has too many possible states. A face under a headset changes with expression, viewpoint, and lighting. A moving body can match a 2D detector in several wrong 3D poses. A point cloud has gaps, so the sign of distance can flip without warning. A deforming surface changes scale from moment to moment, so one fixed texture map cannot know whether detail should follow the material or the screen. Brute force also wastes work in empty or simple regions while still missing small loops, tangencies, self-crossings, and other rare cases that can break later steps.
faces-avatars.mathematical_principle: The recurring idea is to replace blind storage with a rule that answers local questions while respecting whole-object consistency. The rule may be a distance-to-surface value, a smaller set of likely poses for one person, a tree of material regions, a flow that moves every point through time, or an energy score that says how wrong a shape is when it crosses itself, loses a sharp edge, or ignores structural stress. In plain terms, the math is deciding what must stay true while allowing the unknown parts to bend. Some papers compare predicted evidence with camera evidence: projected joints should land near detected joints, or a relit avatar should separate surface color from incoming illumination. Some add many small effects, such as thermal light mixing through a rough surface or wave-like texture changes across a deforming object. Some sample only the places likely to matter, as in ray marching or adaptive surface queries, because checking every point is too slow. The tradeoff is compactness versus trust: a rule is useful only if it can recover detail, uncertainty, and special cases when asked.
faces-avatars.why_math_matters: The math matters because these objects are not just pictures; they have relationships that must survive use. A surface has neighboring parts that should connect. A sharp feature should remain sharp after an offset. A body pose has joints that cannot move independently like loose dots. Illumination on an avatar comes from both skin appearance and the surrounding environment, so changing the room light should not repaint the face itself. A panelized architectural surface must stay close to the intended form while also carrying stress. These are simultaneous demands, and plain hand rules usually fix one while damaging another. Distance fields, explained simply as functions that answer how far a point is from the surface, give a way to find and edit shape without storing every triangle first. Repulsion energies, meaning penalties for parts occupying the same space, help untangle surfaces. Person-specific pose spaces, meaning smaller motion neighborhoods learned for one body, reduce impossible guesses. The common structure is constraint: the result must satisfy many local measurements while still behaving like one coherent object.
faces-avatars.paper_family: The papers connect by choosing different forms for the same missing-object problem. EgoRelight starts from headset cameras and tries to recover an avatar whose appearance can be shown under new lighting, so it must separate what belongs to the person from what belongs to the room. TwinPose starts from many camera views and reduces pose search by using a person-specific space plus a twin pose that carries identity cues. HairGPT treats hair strands as ordered tokens, like a sentence, so it can generate hairstyles by learning which strand shapes tend to follow others. MotionBricks does something similar for motion, building reusable pieces that can be controlled in real time. The surface papers push the same logic into shape storage and repair: PhaseTree keeps multiple material regions in one distance-based construction, SAND spends fewer network layers in easy areas, NeuBase adds editable offsets to a smooth base surface, and Untangling Surfaces penalizes crossings at both broad shape and local element levels. Even thermal hidden-scene imaging belongs here: it reconstructs usable shape from scrambled indirect evidence rather than direct sight, preserving usable evidence.
faces-avatars.what_changed: The 2026 pattern is less about inventing a single representation and more about making representations answer practical questions under pressure. The evidence points to adaptive cost, editability, and separation of mixed causes. SAND and the ray-marching work avoid spending equal compute everywhere. EgoRelight separates lighting from appearance for avatars captured by head-mounted cameras. TwinPose and MotionBricks narrow motion search into controllable spaces instead of solving from scratch every frame. Several surface papers focus on failure cases that used to be treated as cleanup: self-crossings, small intersection loops, tangent contacts, uncertain samples, and sharp offset features. The family is moving from making plausible shapes toward making shapes that can be queried, changed, timed, relit, and checked without collapsing in edge cases.
faces-avatars.limits: These papers depend on the evidence matching their chosen rule. A person-specific pose space can miss unusual motion. A strand-language model for hair can repeat patterns from its examples and may fail on hairstyles outside that experience. Avatar relighting assumes the capture can separate skin appearance, geometry, and environment well enough for new illumination to make sense. Distance-based surfaces and neural surface rules can hide errors where samples are sparse, where signs are ambiguous, or where very thin structures matter. Collision and intersection methods still rely on numerical care, because tiny rounding errors can change whether two surfaces touch. The input file gives problems, approaches, and claimed contributions, not full experiments, so this family explanation can identify the shared logic and assumptions but cannot prove speed, visual quality, or reliability beyond those stated claims.

fluids-smoke-granular.problem_shape: These papers belong together because they all ask how loose, flowing matter can be moved by a computer without losing the physical bookkeeping that makes it believable. Water should carry sand, soak into it, and erode it. Air and water should push on each other across a changing boundary. A painted brush stroke should stir colors sharply instead of turning them into blur. A large flow should keep small swirling detail while using memory a normal machine can afford. A controlled fluid scene should also be adjustable, which means the computer must know how a change made now affects motion many steps later. The shared pressure is that fluids and grains are not single solid objects. Their visible shape comes from many tiny exchanges of volume, push, drift, settling, and mixing. The computer has to chop that continuous motion into cells, particles, samples, or stored displacement rules, then make those pieces agree as time advances. The family is about making that chopping useful without letting it leak water, smear edges, erase vortices, or make design changes too expensive to trace.
fluids-smoke-granular.naive_failure: A smart beginner might draw the surface of the water, slide sand particles downhill, blur colors under a brush, or run one general fluid grid and hope every substance can share it. They might also make the time steps larger to gain speed, or store every detail needed by a high-quality flow method to avoid visual loss. These ideas fail in different-looking but related ways. If water, air, and sand are not coupled carefully, sand can move without the right fluid force, water can vanish from pores, or dry grains can behave like soaked sticky material. If paint mixing is repeatedly resampled, each stroke softens the image. If a fast solver throws away too much state, small swirls disappear. If a control method traces every possible backward influence through a long flow, memory and time explode before the scene can be tuned.
fluids-smoke-granular.mathematical_principle: The recurring mathematical idea is to track what must be carried through motion, then choose a compact way to update it. For sand-water-air mixtures, the carried quantities include fluid volume, grain motion, and water retained inside the granular structure. One method updates fluid behavior with a lattice Boltzmann method, which means it stores small directional flow summaries at grid sites rather than following every molecule, and couples that to a material point method, which means sand is tracked by moving sample points that carry material state. For gas-kinetic fluid solvers, the idea is similar but more compressed: instead of storing many directional distributions, the method evolves moments, meaning bulk summaries such as momentum that describe the crowd behavior of many tiny moving particles. For two-phase flow, the solver must carry both fluid motion and a phase field, a smooth marker telling which liquid is where near the interface. For Mixwell, the stored object is a displacement rule: how an ideal brush tine moves nearby paint. For DiffSurFlow, the stored object is a flow map, a record of how positions travel through time, used to preserve the main routes by which changes affect later motion.
fluids-smoke-granular.why_math_matters: The math matters because flowing materials hide their important structure inside motion, not just shape. A water surface may look like a boundary, but the believable result depends on volume not disappearing, forces passing between phases, and density differences staying stable. Sand may look like grains, but wet sand changes character when liquid enters and remains inside it. A brush stroke may look like a local smear, but sharp mixing depends on moving pigment along clean paths without repeatedly sampling a texture and softening it. A turbulent flow may look random, yet it contains long-lived swirls and paths that carry information across many frames. The repeated mathematical move is therefore conservation plus selective memory. Conservation says that quantities such as volume, momentum, phase identity, and material state should survive a time step unless the modeled physics changes them. Selective memory says the computer should keep the summaries that determine visible behavior and discard redundant detail. That tradeoff, detail versus speed and memory, is the reason these methods use coupled updates, moment summaries, phase markers, displacement functions, and flow-map shortcuts.
fluids-smoke-granular.paper_family: The representative papers are variations on the same deeper move: keep the right history of moving matter while avoiding an impossible amount of bookkeeping. Volume-Preserving LBM-MPM Coupling handles the most literal mixture. It lets air and water evolve as fluids while sand moves as granular material, then makes them exchange forces and preserve volume so settling, transport, erosion, and basin failure do not look like unrelated effects. Kinetic Predicted-Moment Flux Reconstruction and the Extended Full GKS two-phase solver attack the cost of high-quality flow. Both use gas-kinetic reasoning, meaning they describe fluid motion through aggregate particle behavior, but they focus on memory-light updates that still keep fine swirls or sharp two-liquid behavior. Mixwell takes the same concern into 2D painting: instead of solving a full fluid problem after every stroke, it composes brush-induced displacement fields so progressive mixing stays sharp and resolution independent. DiffSurFlow turns the family around from prediction to control. It asks which parts of a long motion carry useful sensitivity backward, then keeps the flow-map connections that act as main influence routes while pruning less useful backward work. Across them, the sibling logic is not the visible material; it is faithful transport under limited computation.
fluids-smoke-granular.what_changed: The 2026 pattern is a push toward fluid methods that are not merely detailed, but practical under hard limits. The evidence emphasizes lower memory, GPU-friendly steps, progressive editing, and long-horizon control. Several papers avoid storing heavy per-point state by using moment summaries, explicit gas-kinetic updates, or displacement functions that compose without intermediate blur. The air-water-sand work adds stronger coupling across materials rather than treating each substance as a separate effect. DiffSurFlow shows another shift: fluids are becoming things to tune and design, not only forward animations to watch. The common change is keeping physically meaningful structure while cutting the cost that usually prevents large scenes, high resolution, or repeated adjustment.
fluids-smoke-granular.limits: The evidence does not show a universal fluid method. Each approach depends on its chosen representation: grid-site flow summaries, moving sand samples, phase markers, analytical brush displacement rules, or flow maps for backward influence. Those choices help when their assumptions match the scene, but can fail outside them. Idealized brush tines may not cover every real paint tool. Moment-based gas-kinetic solvers rely on their summaries preserving the flow details that matter. Two-phase solvers must handle interfaces, density contrasts, and boundaries within their stated models. Coupled sand-water-air behavior assumes the water retention and volume conservation models are adequate. DiffSurFlow assumes the retained flow-map connections really carry the important long-range effects. The abstracts support speed, memory, and example behavior claims, but not every extreme splash, sediment case, turbulent state, brush pattern, or control task.

generative-3d-diffusion.problem_shape: These papers are about asking a computer to make a usable thing when the desired thing is only partly specified. The thing may be a 3D shape, a roof, an indoor room layout, a terrain height map, a character skeleton and motion, a relit video, a chart image, a material transfer, or a segmented object. The shared pressure is that the output cannot be just any plausible picture or shape. It must obey hidden relationships: roofs need connected loops, bodies need joints and contacts, rooms need object relations, terrain needs water and landform consistency, videos need the same person and lighting behavior across time, and generated surfaces need usable vertices and connections. The input is often thin: one image, text, sparse timed light observations, a few user preferences, or an incomplete motion from capture. The family asks how to fill the missing parts by reusing patterns learned from examples while still respecting the specific evidence and controls for the current case.
generative-3d-diffusion.naive_failure: A smart beginner might try to generate the final result all at once from the prompt, image, or partial shape, then repair mistakes afterward. For a room, place objects that look likely. For motion, copy a similar walk and stretch it to the new body. For relighting, repaint each frame. For a surface, predict points or faces in sequence until the object is complete. This fails because the parts are coupled. A later roof vertex depends on earlier roof loops. A person's arm motion depends on body shape, contacts, and timing. A relit frame must agree with neighboring frames. A terrain patch hidden behind a hill must still connect to visible slopes and drainage. Sequential generation also accumulates errors: one bad early decision can force many later decisions into a broken structure.
generative-3d-diffusion.mathematical_principle: The recurring principle is guided denoising and constrained filling-in. Diffusion, in plain terms, starts from a noisy or incomplete version of the answer and repeatedly nudges it toward something that looks like the examples it has learned, while also listening to the current condition such as text, an image, a skeleton, a layout graph, or lighting controls. Flow matching is a related idea: instead of taking many tiny denoising steps, it learns a direction of travel from simple disorder toward structured data. Autoregressive methods make one part after another, but the stronger papers add summaries that keep the growing result aware of larger structure, such as coarse-to-fine shape cells, explicit root motion, or room relations. Across the family, what counts as wrong is not only visual ugliness. Wrongness can mean broken surface connections, poor skeleton-motion agreement, inconsistent lighting over time, height maps that violate landform cues, adapter weights that users dislike, or generated parts that disagree across views. The math supplies a controlled path from uncertainty to a specific structured answer, while deciding at each step which evidence should steer the next change.
generative-3d-diffusion.why_math_matters: This math matters because the missing information is not random. Shapes, rooms, bodies, faces, materials, charts, and light have repeated structure that can be learned, but each task also has constraints that examples alone cannot guarantee. A chair in a room must relate to walls and other objects. A character's motion must fit the character's body rather than only the word walk. A quad layout, meaning a surface divided into four-sided patches for editing, must remain simple enough for artists to use. A height map must explain both visible terrain and hidden regions. A video relighting method must change illumination without changing identity or flickering from frame to frame. The mathematical tools give the generator memory and steering. Attention routes information between image and text tokens, relation graphs carry room structure, masked filling repairs chosen regions, and preference search turns a user's choices into better model-mixing weights. The tradeoff is freedom versus obedience: the model needs enough freedom to invent missing detail, but enough constraint to keep the invented detail usable.
generative-3d-diffusion.paper_family: The representative papers are siblings because each turns generation into structured repair rather than free invention. A Few-Step Generative Model on Cumulative Flow Maps and Orbit-Space Particle Flow Matching focus on the path itself: how to travel from disorder to a finished sample in fewer, straighter, less noisy moves. Grow3D and Nexus apply the same pressure to 3D shapes, avoiding slow or error-prone one-piece-at-a-time generation by predicting coarse-to-fine cells, vertices, and connection information more holistically. SQuadGen, Loops2Roofs, CasLayout, Pixels2Peaks, and Tempo3D show the geometric branch: the output must satisfy layout, loop, view, terrain, or multi-view structure, not merely look like a shape. ACT, DMP, MotionBricks, Autoregressive Diffusion for human motion, virtual try-on, and MOCHI move the family into bodies, garments, contacts, and control. GenPIE uses generative priors to bridge sparse timed light observations, while BodyReLux and Pixel Cube use video generation to relight people without losing temporal agreement. GimmBO, HeadRouter, DealMaTe, HumanFlow, UniVidX, pictorial chart generation, SegviGen, and StyleID show the same idea for editing, control, material, video, segmentation, and identity: learned image-making must be tied to structure that can be checked.
generative-3d-diffusion.what_changed: The 2026 pattern is that generative graphics is becoming less satisfied with pretty unconstrained output. The evidence emphasizes fewer generation steps, real-time or interactive control, and outputs that carry usable structure. Shape papers care about vertices, connections, coarse-to-fine cells, loops, and quad layouts. Motion papers care about streaming control, body differences, contacts, and text or kinematic constraints. Imaging and relighting papers mix learned guesses with sparse measurements, lighting tokens, masks, or view consistency. Another change is that generative models are being reused outside pure synthesis: for segmentation, virtual try-on, material transfer, adapter merging, identity measurement, and chart design. The family is moving from making examples to making editable, constrained assets.
generative-3d-diffusion.limits: The evidence does not prove that these methods understand every possible object, body, room, material, or lighting situation. Learned generators depend on examples and may fail when a new case falls outside those patterns, such as unusual creatures, rare roof styles, unfamiliar garments, extreme terrain, or lighting not represented in training data. Constraint signals can also be incomplete or wrong: a single image may not determine 3D shape, sparse light observations may support multiple scenes, and user preferences may be inconsistent. Faster few-step methods may trade some correction time for speed. The abstracts report contributions more than failure cases, so they do not establish reliability under severe occlusion, bad prompts, heavy motion, unusual topology, or physical interactions beyond the stated constraints.

geometry-processing-meshes.problem_shape: These papers are about making digital shape behave like a trustworthy object instead of a loose collection of samples. A mesh, meaning a surface stored as many small connected triangles or quads, may need to be measured, cleaned, simplified, animated, printed, textured, cut into panels, or compared with another surface. The shared difficulty is that the visible object is continuous, but the computer often holds it as pieces: vertices, faces, rays, fields, slices, correspondences, tokens, or captured points. If the pieces are changed independently, the object can tear, cross itself, lose sharp edges, blur texture, break inside-out tests, or become too slow to query. The family therefore keeps asking the same question in different forms: what relationships must remain true while the representation changes? Some papers preserve appearance while remaking triangles, some preserve distance or winding tests while accelerating queries, some preserve cloth, garment, skeleton, or toolpath structure while adapting shape to motion or manufacture. The common object is not just a shape, but a shape plus the rules that make it usable.
geometry-processing-meshes.naive_failure: A smart beginner might try to treat every small piece of geometry separately. To compare two surfaces, check every triangle against every other triangle. To clean a tangled surface, push intersecting faces apart locally. To preserve a texture, keep the old image and hope the new triangles still line up. To generate an artist-style surface, list faces one by one. To print a non-planar object, slice it into simple layers and connect nearby paths. These attempts fail because shape errors are relational. A small local fix can create a global wrongness: an inside becomes outside, a sharp feature rounds off, a garment no longer matches a body, a cloth frame no longer agrees with nearby frames, or a toolpath collides after a layer looks valid by itself. Brute force also fails at scale. Exact distance, winding, intersection, and surface evaluation become expensive when every query must inspect too many pieces.
geometry-processing-meshes.mathematical_principle: The recurring principle is to turn shape into constraints that can be measured and preserved while the representation changes. Distance methods measure the worst mismatch between two surfaces, then avoid useless work by proving that whole regions cannot contain the answer. Winding-number methods measure whether a point is inside by adding the signed influence of the surrounding surface, then reduce that addition to faster ray or boundary calculations. Remeshing and offsetting preserve visible appearance, sharp features, and correspondence, meaning the new pieces must still point back to the same parts of the old object. Untangling and panelization adjust vertices or surface flows while penalizing intersections, stress, or loss of fidelity. Generation and capture papers use fields, correspondences, and aggregations to carry hidden structure such as skeletons, skin weights, garment-body matches, wrinkle motion, or surface signals. The math matters because it defines what counts as wrong: too far away, crossing when it should not, losing an edge, changing density, breaking endpoint distributions, or violating toolpath thickness. Once wrongness is measurable, algorithms can search, subdivide, simplify, or stop early with a reason.
geometry-processing-meshes.why_math_matters: The mathematics is not decoration because surfaces contain structure that the eye, the printer, the simulator, and downstream tools all depend on. A triangle list alone does not say which side is inside, which edge is intentionally sharp, which texture sample belongs to which point, or whether two nearby folds are allowed to touch. Boundary integrals, ray tests, Hausdorff bounds, convex hulls, and Lipschitz limits give ways to make claims about entire pieces of shape instead of guessing from individual samples. Energy terms, which are scores that rise when a surface bends, intersects, drifts, or carries stress badly, let several demands be balanced at once. Differential operators and harmonic maps describe how quantities change across a surface, so smoothing, curvature, uncertainty, and constant-curvature design can be handled as surface behavior rather than image cleanup. Fields are useful because they assign values throughout space or over a domain, which lets printing paths, skeleton confidence, fabric fibers, or generated signals be followed continuously instead of as disconnected decisions.
geometry-processing-meshes.paper_family: The representative papers fit together because each protects a different relationship while changing or querying geometry. Texture-Aware Remeshing changes the triangle layout but moves texture information onto vertices so later geometry operations still see appearance. Iskra asks how existing geometry programs can run backward, so a desired output can tell the input shape how to change. The winding-number papers and the Hausdorff-distance papers make inside-out and surface-distance questions faster by replacing exhaustive checks with ray tests, boundary formulas, branch-and-bound, buffers, moments, and certified subdivision. Feature-Preserving Offset Meshing, the NURBS intersection algorithm, Structural MAT, and Subgrid Marching Tetrahedra all guard structural details while deriving new surfaces, intersections, skeleton-like medial descriptions, or fine sheets from imperfect discrete input. Untangling Surfaces and Stress-Aware Panelization score the shape against physical or geometric violations, then adjust it to remove crossings or balance stress and fidelity. Strips as Tokens, Matern Noise, AniGen, Tempo3D, ACT, and virtual try-on bring the same concern into learned generation: the output must carry connections, UV boundaries, skeletons, motion, or garment correspondences, not just look plausible. Cloth capture, fabric capture, kirigami, AtomSlicer, and MorphSkein show the same logic when shape must obey cameras, fibers, cuts, print beads, or pixel density.
geometry-processing-meshes.what_changed: The 2026 pattern in this evidence is that geometry processing is less isolated from the rest of graphics. Classical questions such as distance, intersection, inside-out tests, remeshing, offsets, medial axes, and curvature are still present, but they are being pushed onto GPUs, made certified, or connected to uncertainty. At the same time, generated and captured shapes are expected to arrive with usable structure: UV boundaries, skeletons, skinning, garment correspondences, cloth motion, fabric fibers, and surface signals. Fabrication and display papers also demand geometry that respects physical constraints such as bead thickness, deployability, stress, collision freedom, and pixel density. The shift is from producing a surface to producing a surface that remains actionable.
geometry-processing-meshes.limits: The evidence does not prove a single universal geometry method. Many results depend on assumptions about the input: triangle meshes, NURBS curves and patches, UV parameterization, clean or dirty surfaces, high-resolution meshes, microscopic images, bracketed exposures, planar graphs, or known garment and body proxies. Several approaches rely on discretization, floating-point arithmetic, learned models, or simulators, so their guarantees may weaken outside the tested setting. Speedups for winding numbers, Hausdorff distance, neural surface queries, or hair scattering do not automatically transfer to every model size, tolerance, hardware layout, or visual case. The abstracts also state contributions more than failures. They do not fully establish behavior on extreme self-intersections, missing texture evidence, unusual skeletons, severe capture occlusion, unsupported materials, or fabrication machines with different physical limits.

neural-fields-representations.problem_shape: These papers belong together because they ask how a computer can store something that is spread continuously through space, time, direction, or material, while still answering local questions quickly. The stored thing may be a volume seen by a camera ray, a surface that can be pulled by an artist, a lattice material whose small cells decide whole-part stiffness, a hidden thermal scene mixed by a rough wall, a portrait whose lighting must change over time, or a point cloud that should behave like a solid shape. A direct stored grid is wasteful because most places are simple, empty, smooth, or repeated, while a few places carry sharp edges, contacts, lighting changes, or mechanical detail. A plain learned rule can be compact, but it may be slow to ask at every point and hard to edit. The family problem is therefore representation under pressure: keep enough hidden structure to recover surfaces, images, forces, color, or motion, but avoid storing or querying every possible sample.
neural-fields-representations.naive_failure: A smart beginner would choose one uniform description and push it hard. Store a dense table of values everywhere. March a ray in tiny equal steps. Ask the same neural network at every point. Smooth every surface because smooth functions are easy to learn. Fit soft blobs to a volume and draw them all at every viewing scale. Or let a learned surrogate replace a physics solver without respecting the solver's coarse-to-fine structure. These attempts fail because the world is uneven. Empty space and flat regions do not need the same work as a sharp boundary. Smooth models blur jumps and corners. Uniform sampling wastes effort away from surfaces and misses thin features if the step size is too large. A fast learned material solver can be useless if its errors are unstable by engineering standards.
neural-fields-representations.mathematical_principle: The recurring mathematical principle is adaptive representation: describe a continuous object with smaller pieces whose cost follows the local difficulty of the question. In plain terms, each method builds a map that can be asked, what is here, what direction matters here, how much detail is needed here, or can this region be skipped. Gabor Fields use oriented wave-like filters, meaning small directional pattern detectors, so volume detail can be kept or pruned by viewing scale and direction. SAND lets easy spatial locations stop early when a learned surface rule has already answered enough. Bounding stratified Bernoulli impulses groups random yes-or-no surface events into regions, then uses bounds to avoid marching through points that cannot change the result. NeuBase puts learned offsets on top of a smooth editable base surface, so deformation has local handles instead of becoming a black box. GMT follows multigrid logic, where a hard physical solve is handled from coarse structure to fine correction. Across the family, wrongness means lost detail, slow queries, broken edit behavior, unstable residual error, missed surfaces, or a mismatch to measured images, materials, or physical response.
neural-fields-representations.why_math_matters: The math matters because the underlying signals are not random piles of numbers. Surfaces usually change smoothly until they reach an edge or branch. Volume detail has scale and direction: a broad cloudy region and a thin stripe should not cost the same. A point cloud gives scattered evidence of a surface, but nearby points and local curvature help decide inside, outside, offsets, and Boolean shape operations. Composite layers and lattice microstructures have repeated small structure whose whole-object stiffness can be predicted only if the small cells are averaged in a controlled way. Light, color, and thermal measurements are mixtures, so a method must separate causes before it can relight, reconstruct, or display them. Adaptive depth, bounds, basis functions, multigrid levels, sparse singularities, tensor factors, and local torus fits are different bookkeeping tools for the same tradeoff: compact storage versus trustworthy recovery. They work when the chosen structure matches the real regularity in the scene, material, surface, sensor, or physical system.
neural-fields-representations.paper_family: The representative papers are siblings because each makes a continuous field more queryable without treating every location alike. Gabor Fields, Soft Anisotropic Diagrams, and neural quadrature all decide where detail or samples deserve spending: by orientation and scale for volumes, by soft spatial cells for images, or by learned sample placement for integration. SAND, the Bernoulli-impulse ray marcher, DCx, Points as Tori, and SharpNet all focus on surfaces whose answers must be fast but cannot erase sharp or unusual structure; they differ in whether they skip easy regions, extract an explicit surface, fit local distance shapes, or add controlled jumps to a learned function. NeuBase and explicit flows make learned shape descriptions editable by giving them base surfaces or invertible motion paths. GMT and the laminated-composite paper move the same idea into engineering: represent physical response or manufacturable layers as fields that can be solved or adjusted efficiently. EgoRelight, Pixel Cube, PAColorHolo, thermal hidden-scene imaging, Schlieren flow reconstruction, and material modeling show the imaging branch, where the field stores appearance, light, color, flow, or uncertainty so new views, lighting, or reconstructions can be asked for later.
neural-fields-representations.what_changed: The 2026 pattern is that neural fields are being judged less as clever compact containers and more as working parts inside editing, rendering, capture, and engineering systems. The evidence emphasizes fast queries, early exits, region bounds, direct deformation, explicit surface extraction, controlled sharp features, manufacturable layers, and solver-level accuracy. Another change is selectivity. Rather than using the same network depth, sample pattern, or volume detail everywhere, many papers adapt computation to local complexity, direction, scale, uncertainty, or perceptual importance. The family is also spreading beyond view synthesis into materials, holographic color, hidden thermal imaging, flow reconstruction, pose, motion retargeting, radiation pressure, and composite design.
neural-fields-representations.limits: The evidence does not prove a universal representation for all geometry, light, material, motion, and physics. Many methods depend on the field having the kind of structure their shortcut expects: directional volume detail, locally smooth surfaces, reliable bounds, editable subdivision bases, sparse lattice hierarchies, usable point normals, recoverable lighting, or training examples close to the test case. Adaptive methods can fail if they skip a rare feature that later matters. Smooth learned functions still need special handling for discontinuities, branches, or non-manifold cases, meaning places where a surface connection is not the simple sheet-like case. Solver surrogates must keep residual errors within task requirements, not just look plausible. The abstracts report contributions and selected numbers, but not complete failure behavior under severe noise, extreme topology, unusual materials, unsupported sensors, or deployment constraints.

neural-rendering-radiance-fields.problem_shape: These papers belong together because they all try to turn scattered visual or physical evidence into something that can be viewed, edited, measured, or reused quickly. The evidence may be a few camera views from a headset, one microscope image of woven fabric, sparse X-ray projections, timed laser returns, samples from a ray tracer, soft 3D blobs used to stand in for a scene, or stored values inside a compact spatial data structure. The hard part is that the thing being represented is richer than the measurements. A face has skin color and outside lighting mixed together. A blurry capture has lens focus mixed with scene depth. A volume has empty space, fine detail, and changing viewing distance. A hidden scene or flow field is seen only through indirect distortion. The shared family problem is therefore not simply making an image. It is building a compact, queryable account of how light, shape, material, or density behaves, then asking that account for new views, new lighting, forces, gradients, or display output without recomputing every microscopic event.
neural-rendering-radiance-fields.naive_failure: A smart beginner would store or test everything uniformly. They might march along every ray at the same spacing, evaluate the same neural network at every point, keep every soft scene blob, sample every pixel equally, fit a face video directly to the observed colors, or increase resolution after a sparse render. This breaks because visual importance is uneven. Empty space does not need the same work as a surface edge. A sharp discontinuity cannot be represented well by a model that prefers smooth changes. A million tiny blobs cannot all be drawn expensively at interactive speed. A single photograph of fabric does not reveal every fiber unless the weave pattern is also constrained. Direct fitting can also confuse causes: lighting, material, geometry, focus blur, and sensor mixing can produce similar images, so matching pixels alone may choose the wrong explanation.
neural-rendering-radiance-fields.mathematical_principle: The recurring mathematical idea is adaptive representation: keep enough information to answer the next visual question, but spend detail only where the scene or measurement demands it. In everyday terms, the methods divide the world into places, directions, scales, times, or samples, then decide which parts deserve more care. Ray marching through a learned surface can skip regions whose bounds prove they cannot matter. Adaptive network depth stops evaluating a point once the easy part of the scene has been resolved. Sampling methods choose more rays or image locations where mistakes would be visible, instead of spreading effort evenly. Caches store incoming light estimates so later inverse rendering can compare a proposed scene against images with less random noise. Soft blobs, Gabor kernels, spherical grids, compact trees, and diagram cells are different storage shapes for the same goal: approximate a continuous visual field with pieces that can be combined quickly. The adjustable quantities include color, density, lighting, material labels, force response, fiber parameters, neural weights, and spatial cells.
