What counts as wrong is a mismatch to captured images, noisy derivatives, lost sharp features, excessive storage, slow traversal, or a failure to stay consistent across time and lighting.
neural-rendering-radiance-fields.why_math_matters: The math matters because light and shape have exploitable structure. Nearby points often look related, but edges, fibers, silhouettes, focus blur, and material boundaries can change suddenly. Empty regions along a ray can be skipped, yet a thin surface must not be missed. Many small light paths must be added, but most are unimportant for a particular pixel or force query. A moving avatar must keep the same person while separating skin appearance from illumination. A hidden thermal scene is mixed by a rough surface in a repeatable way, and sparse X-ray views still constrain possible material volumes. These methods use that structure as bookkeeping. Bounds say when a region is safe to ignore. Frequencies describe coarse versus fine detail, like separating a broad wash from a sharp stripe. Differentiable rendering, meaning rendering that also tells how the image would change if an unknown changed, gives inverse tasks a direction for correction. Learned models supply patterns from examples, while physical or spatial constraints keep those patterns tied to the measured scene.
neural-rendering-radiance-fields.paper_family: The representative papers are siblings because they choose smarter questions to ask of a scene representation. Bounding stratified Bernoulli impulses and SAND both reduce wasted point queries: one bounds ray-marched surface regions, the other lets easy locations exit a neural surface network early. Gaussian Point Splatting, closed-form defocus for Gaussian Splatting, Gabor Fields, and Soft Anisotropic Diagrams all reshape soft point or image pieces so they can draw many samples, handle scale, blur, or neighborhood influence without paying the full cost everywhere. EgoRelight, Pixel Cube, and the facial delighting work separate identity or reflectance from lighting so a captured person can be relit instead of merely replayed. Radiance caching, sample matching, boundary path integrals, neural quadrature, and adaptive path tracing attack the same noise problem: estimates of light or derivatives become useful only when samples are chosen, paired, or reused carefully. GenPIE, thermal non-line-of-sight imaging, Schlieren tomography, and discrete X-ray tomography infer hidden 3D or time-varying structure from sparse measurements. Fabric capture, feather appearance, hair scattering, radiation pressure, neutron transport, and holography show the same family logic beyond ordinary pictures: compact light-aware models must remain fast enough for design, display, or editing.
neural-rendering-radiance-fields.what_changed: The 2026 pattern is less about inventing a single new scene format and more about making learned visual representations obey practical pressure. The evidence emphasizes speed, selective work, and inverse use: real-time splatting at huge scale, adaptive sampling below one sample per pixel, compact spatial storage, early exits in neural surfaces, and cached or paired estimates for steadier gradients. It also pushes these representations into capture and control. Headset avatars, portrait relighting, fabric from a microscope image, sparse tomography, hidden-scene imaging, holography, and spacecraft force design all ask the same stored visual account to support new lighting, new views, physical forces, or unknown-scene recovery.
neural-rendering-radiance-fields.limits: The evidence does not show a representation that works for every scene, material, sensor, or display. Many methods depend on specific capture conditions: stereo depth cameras in a headset, a single microscopic fabric image, sparse X-ray angles, time-resolved laser hardware, blurry Gaussian-splat captures, or training data that teaches a relighting prior. Speedups often assume that skipped regions, cached values, compressed cells, or simplified scattering still preserve the visually or physically important parts. Learned models may fail outside their examples, and inverse tasks can remain ambiguous when lighting, material, depth, and density explain the same measurements. The abstracts report claimed improvements, not full stress tests under unusual motion, extreme occlusion, unsupported materials, severe noise, or deployment limits.

physical-simulation.problem_shape: These papers belong together because they all try to make a digital world obey ordinary physical expectations while staying fast enough to use. Sand should settle instead of vanishing, water should push air and grains aside, a thin sheet should bend without looking rubbery, yarn should hold loops, cloth should match a moving body, wood decay should follow grain and moisture, and a robot motion should respect balance and contact. The shared problem is that real matter is continuous and crowded, while the computer must break it into points, cells, particles, bodies, samples, or learned shortcuts. Each small piece has local rules, but the viewer notices global failures: lost volume, jitter, blur, self-crossing, wrong bending, unstable contact, or motion that no real body could perform. The family is therefore about carrying physical bookkeeping through change. It asks what must be preserved as time advances: mass, volume, momentum, contact separation, bend resistance, heat exchange, force from light, or agreement between a captured or designed object and how it could actually move.
physical-simulation.naive_failure: A smart beginner might animate the visible surface directly: move vertices where the artist wants them, blur colors to show mixing, push interpenetrating objects apart, or take bigger time steps to make the scene faster. For fluids, they might store water, air, and sand on one grid and hope the parts share space cleanly. For cloth or shells, they might penalize stretching and add a simple bending score. For robots or garments, they might copy motion from one body to another. These ideas fail because physical mistakes accumulate. A tiny loss of volume becomes draining water or shrinking sand. A local contact fix can create new intersections nearby. Large time steps skip over collisions or smear free surfaces. A copied motion can put a foot through the floor or ask a joint to do impossible work. The hard part is not moving things; it is moving them while honoring many coupled rules at once.
physical-simulation.mathematical_principle: The recurring math idea is to turn physical behavior into quantities that can be checked, balanced, and carried forward through time. Some papers add up many small effects: random photon paths become radiation pressure, many possible heat paths become a temperature boundary answer, and many fluid or sand samples become bulk motion. Some split a hard problem into easier agreements: yarn constraints, contact rules, body joints, or distributed regions are solved separately and then forced to match. Some search for settings that reduce wrongness, where wrongness means lost volume, mismatched captured cloth, unbalanced load across machines, a body drifting from a reference motion, or a shape crossing itself. Some replace expensive detail with a smaller but faithful summary: moment-space flow, low-rank deformation modes, fixed integration points, precomputed matrices, or a learned proxy that answers force queries quickly. The plain principle is conservation plus correction. Conservation says certain totals or relationships should not disappear when the clock ticks. Correction says that when the computer's rough pieces disagree, the method measures the disagreement and pushes the pieces back toward a physically believable state.
physical-simulation.why_math_matters: The math matters because physical scenes have hidden structure that a picture alone does not contain. Water and sand can look like a moving boundary, but underneath they exchange volume and push on each other. A shell can look like a surface, but its bending depends on how nearby patches rotate, not just where points sit. Knitwear can look like cloth, but each yarn loop constrains neighboring loops. A terrain river is shaped by rare transport events over long times, not just one local velocity. Contact needs inequality rules: two things may touch, but their interiors should not occupy the same place. Time stepping needs stability rules: the next frame should not create more energy, mass loss, or visual noise just because the step was large. These papers exploit structure in the world: matter is locally connected, forces add up, constraints repeat, slow and fast processes can be separated, and many systems can be summarized without tracking every microscopic detail. That is why counting, sampling, partitioning, solving, and correction are central rather than decorative.
physical-simulation.paper_family: The representative papers show the same family logic across very different materials. Air-water-sand coupling, two-phase flow, fast free-surface flow, high-order fluid flow, VEM fluids, Mixwell, and terrain erosion all track how material moves through space without losing sharp boundaries, volume, or long-time structure. Better Bending, yarn-level knitwear, cloth capture, virtual try-on, origami materials, and deformation models ask how thin or soft things can bend, fold, wrinkle, or fit bodies while respecting contact and material limits. YASPS, M-ABD, heterogeneous subspace corrections, MPM Lite, JGS2-GQ, and low-rank Koopman deformables are about making large physical solves cheaper by reusing structure, splitting work, or shrinking the number of active unknowns. Radiation pressure, neutron transport, holography, time-of-flight rendering, and nonlinear heat boundaries add many uncertain paths of light, particles, or heat, then use sampling or learned shortcuts to make design questions practical. Surface untangling and distributed partitioning protect the surrounding pipeline: if shape crosses itself or work is divided badly, later physical steps fail. Even procedural deforming texture belongs here because it tries to keep surface detail physically plausible under extreme stretching without running a full physical solve.
physical-simulation.what_changed: The 2026 version of this family is not just chasing more detailed motion. The evidence points to methods that keep physical bookkeeping while reducing cost: larger time steps, lower memory, fewer active particles, precomputed matrices, smaller deformation summaries, and GPU-friendly formulas. It also shows more crossing between physical animation, capture, design, robotics, rendering, and fabrication. A solver may now support virtual try-on, cloth capture, spacecraft force design, nuclear shielding, haptic proxy choice, or distributed film production. Another change is concern for extensibility and verification: bending models are compared systematically, contact derivatives are generated symbolically, and partitioning includes temporal consistency. The emphasis is shifting from isolated demos toward physical answers that can survive inside larger workflows.
physical-simulation.limits: The evidence does not prove that one physical method handles all materials or scales. Many papers assume a particular representation, such as grids, particles, affine bodies, yarn curves, shell patches, captured cloth templates, crease patterns, or proxy human bodies. Sampling methods depend on enough samples to tame noise. Learned shortcuts depend on training cases or proxy models staying close to the new query. Large time steps, reduced summaries, and fixed integration points can miss small events if their assumptions break. Contact and coupling methods also rely on numerical tolerances and clean enough input. The abstracts report contributions, not full failure maps, so they do not establish behavior on every extreme splash, knot, fracture, garment layer, robot body, lighting condition, machine layout, or biological material.

rendering-light-transport.problem_shape: These papers belong together because they all chase light after it becomes hard to count directly. A scene, a face, a cloud of hair, a hologram, a hidden object, or a phone snapshot is shaped by many tiny light events: leaving a source, bouncing, scattering, being blocked, arriving late, spreading through glass, or mixing across a rough surface. The computer or camera only sees a small part of that story. It may record a few exposures, a headset view, a delayed flash return, a sparse laser scan, or a noisy set of ray samples. The shared problem is to recover or predict the full visual result without measuring every possible route light could take. That makes the family wider than ordinary image making. Some papers render pictures, some infer lighting or material from video, some simulate time-of-flight sensors, holograms, hair, feathers, neutrons, X-rays, or radiation pressure. They are siblings because each turns incomplete light evidence into a believable account of what happened between source, scene, and sensor.
rendering-light-transport.naive_failure: A smart beginner would try to follow everything evenly. Shoot the same number of rays through every pixel, test every point along a ray, sample every time delay, gather every hair bounce, or blend every exposure with a fixed rule. For inverse tasks, they might change material, shape, or lighting until the rendered image looks close to the captured one. This fails because most possible light routes matter little, while a few cause sharp highlights, shadow edges, hidden-depth clues, bright display points, or important forces. Equal effort wastes samples in calm regions and misses rare paths. Direct fitting also becomes unstable: the same image can be explained by different lighting, material, or geometry, and small random errors can point the adjustment in the wrong direction.
rendering-light-transport.mathematical_principle: The recurring math idea is controlled addition under uncertainty. Rendering and imaging ask for a sum of many possible contributions, but the contributions are too numerous to list. Random sampling, meaning choosing a manageable set of representative light paths or sensor events, estimates the sum without visiting everything. The important question is where to spend those choices and how to keep their noise from overwhelming the answer. Several papers bound regions, reuse nearby or previous paths, match samples so opposite errors cancel, cache values for later reuse, or choose more samples where the viewer will notice mistakes. In inverse work, the adjusted quantity may be facial color, lighting, volume density, material, shielding shape, X-ray material labels, or a force model. A score measures what is wrong: an image mismatch, a noisy derivative, a broken time gate, a wrong exposure, a missing hidden scene, or a display point that is too dim. The method then changes the unknowns in the direction that reduces that measured wrongness while staying tied to the physics of light travel, so the final estimate is not just visually plausible but constrained by measurements.
rendering-light-transport.why_math_matters: This math matters because light has structure even when it looks chaotic. It moves along paths; later arrivals usually traveled farther; nearby pixels and nearby frames often share useful paths; dense hair and feathers can be treated partly as a volume that scatters light; a rough surface mixes hidden thermal evidence in a repeatable way; a phone bracket has multiple versions of the same scene at different brightness levels. The papers exploit those patterns instead of treating every measurement as unrelated. Time-of-flight rendering reuses paths only after respecting path length. Adaptive path tracing, meaning image making by tracing possible light routes, spends effort where sparse samples would be most visible. Gradient estimators, which estimate how the answer changes when a scene value changes, reduce noise by coupling terms that should cancel. Holographic and volumetric display work must obey wave or laser constraints, not just paint pixels. The mathematical machinery is therefore a bookkeeping system for what light is allowed to do and which missing pieces can be inferred.
rendering-light-transport.paper_family: The representative papers connect through this same bookkeeping. GenPIE and thermal non-line-of-sight imaging start from sparse or mixed sensor evidence and try to reconstruct hidden or high-dimensional light behavior, using learned priors only where the captured evidence is insufficient. EgoRelight, Pixel Cube, BodyReLux, and the facial delighting work separate a person from the lighting on that person so the same face or body can be shown under new illumination. ToF ReSTIR and HoloPathTracer adapt path tracing to harder timing or wave-display constraints, while the dual-path volumetric display turns controlled laser paths into visible 3D points. Hair, fur, and feather papers simplify many fiber interactions without discarding the look of repeated scattering. Radiance caching, meaning storing estimates of incoming light, sample matching, boundary path integrals, and differentiable transport, meaning computing how the result changes when a design changes, all ask how to get less noisy guidance when matching a target. Lucky HDR combines bracketed phone exposures without hallucinating. Spherical-grid products, Gabor fields, Gaussian point splatting, where soft blobs stand in for scene pieces, defocus convolution, and compact spatial data structures address the same pressure from another side: store or combine light-related information so queries stay fast enough.
rendering-light-transport.what_changed: The 2026 pattern is that light transport is no longer only about making a final still image. The evidence shows rendering ideas moving into capture, displays, phone cameras, tomography, neutron transport, spacecraft force design, relightable avatars, and hidden-scene imaging. Another change is the focus on extreme scarcity: below one sample per pixel, sparse laser observations, limited-angle X-rays, few exposure brackets, and real-time headset or display constraints. Learned models appear often, but the stronger pattern is hybrid: learned guesses are checked against timing, exposure, path length, scattering, wave behavior, material separation, sensor physics, or display hardware limits before they are trusted.
rendering-light-transport.limits: The evidence does not prove that these methods work for arbitrary scenes or sensors. Many papers assume particular hardware, such as head-mounted stereo cameras, laser-detector setups, single-photon sensors, femtosecond lasers, phone exposure brackets, or X-ray views. Others rely on training data, learned priors, cached estimates, bounded surface behavior, or simplified hair, feather, volume, wave, and force models. A method that reduces noise for one derivative or sample pattern may not help another. The abstracts also report contributions more than failure cases, so they do not establish behavior under severe occlusion, unusual materials, changing illumination, unsupported display brightness, extreme motion, or real deployment limits.

sketching-vector-2d.problem_shape: This family is about drawings that must behave like structured objects, not just colored marks on a page. A stroke in an animation may pass behind another stroke and reappear later. A curve cut out of a three-dimensional scene may need to say clearly which line is in front. A smooth color boundary in vector art may need to spread tone across a region without breaking at the edge. A texture pasted on a shape may need to survive later edits to that shape. The shared pressure is that two-dimensional visual work often has hidden order underneath it: layers, crossings, surfaces, color boundaries, and time. A flat picture can look simple to the viewer while being hard for a computer because the drawing has to remember which parts connect, which parts block others, and which changes preserve the intended appearance. These papers belong together because they try to turn hand-drawn or vector-like marks into reliable structures that can be animated, intersected, rendered, edited, or connected back to three-dimensional form.
sketching-vector-2d.naive_failure: A smart first attempt would treat every visible line or color patch as independent. For animation, match each stroke in one drawing to the nearest stroke in the next drawing and blend their positions. For 3D vectorization, project curves onto the image and sort them afterward. For surface intersections, sample many points and connect the ones that seem close. For textured shapes, edit the shape and hope the texture follows. These shortcuts fail when important information is hidden at the exact places where drawings are most useful: crossings, tangencies, occlusions, small loops, and boundaries. Nearby strokes may not be the same object. A line can disappear because it is behind another line, not because it ends. Tiny intersection loops can be missed by sparse sampling. Texture coordinates can preserve a picture poorly after the shape is changed. The failure is not just visual mess; it is loss of the relationships that make the drawing editable.
sketching-vector-2d.mathematical_principle: The repeated mathematical idea is to replace loose pixels or loose strokes with relationships that can be checked. Some papers ask what should stay connected as a line moves through time. Some ask how a flat plane is divided when many projected curves cross. Some ask whether a tiny closed intersection loop exists even when ordinary point sampling misses it. Some ask how color should spread from boundary curves into the empty space between them. In everyday terms, the math acts like bookkeeping for promises: this stroke continues here, this region lies in front of that one, this curve enters and leaves a patch, this surface color should remain attached to the visible shape, and this color field should satisfy the boundary conditions set by the drawn curves. The tools differ. Winding numbers count how a path wraps around a point so hidden loops can be detected. Subdivision repeatedly cuts a hard region into smaller regions until its structure is easier to decide. Monte Carlo sampling spends random trials on estimating many small contributions instead of tracing every possible influence. The common tradeoff is freedom versus consistency: artists want flexible marks, but the computer needs enough structure to avoid broken crossings, wrong layers, and unstable edits.
sketching-vector-2d.why_math_matters: The math matters because vector and sketch-like graphics are full of exact-looking events that are easy to damage. A crossing is not just two dark marks touching; it decides which curve continues, which region is separated, and which part may be hidden. A tangent contact, where two surfaces just brush, can be more fragile than a clean crossing because a tiny numerical error can turn contact into a miss or a false overlap. A diffusion curve is not only a line with colors on its sides; it asks the surrounding area to fill itself smoothly from those boundary instructions. A texture on a shape is not merely an image pasted on top; later tools must know how the appearance travels with the shape. These papers need counting, partitioning, repeated refinement, and solving because the important facts are relational. They live between marks: inside or outside, before or behind, connected or separated, preserved or changed. Hand-written rules tend to fail at special cases, while mathematical checks give the system a way to notice when several visual promises must all be true at once.
sketching-vector-2d.paper_family: LayerInbetween represents the time side of the family: it treats inbetweening as more than sliding strokes between drawings, because occluded strokes require a predicted layer order and a correspondence between marks that may not always be visible. Robust Planar Maps for 3D Vectorization represents the projection side: it turns curve soup from a three-dimensional scene into a valid flat division, so lines, intersections, and occlusions can be handled as an organized map rather than as independent curves. The NURBS surface intersection paper handles a related crossing problem on smooth designed surfaces, where small loops and tangent intersections can vanish unless the method reasons about wrapping and subdivides the search carefully. Texture-Aware Remeshing moves the same concern into surface editing: it tries to keep appearance attached to geometry by carrying texture information onto vertices before later processing. Monte Carlo Rendering of Biharmonic Diffusion Curves handles the color-spreading side of vector graphics, using random estimates and a solved boundary problem to render smooth fields from curve instructions. Across these examples, the deeper move is the same: turn a drawing-like object into a structure whose hidden connections, regions, and boundary promises can survive computation.
sketching-vector-2d.what_changed: The 2026 version of this family seems less focused on making vector graphics merely cleaner and more focused on making them dependable under hard operations. The evidence points to occlusion-aware animation, valid planar maps for projected 3D curves, intersection handling for tiny loops and tangent contacts, texture-aware geometry processing, and stochastic rendering for higher-order diffusion curves. In plain terms, the work is moving toward cases where simple drawings meet demanding pipelines: animation editing, CAD-like surface intersection, 3D-to-2D conversion, textured shape processing, and smooth vector color rendering. The change is reliability under ambiguity: preserving layers, crossings, appearance, and boundary behavior when the input is incomplete, crowded, or numerically delicate.
sketching-vector-2d.limits: These family claims depend on the input having enough structure for the chosen checks to mean something. Stroke correspondence still assumes that there is a recoverable relation between drawings, even when some marks are hidden. Planar maps and intersection methods assume curves and surfaces are described accurately enough that crossings, loops, and tangencies can be detected rather than buried in bad input. Texture-aware processing assumes appearance can be carried through vertex colors without losing the details that matter for the later tool. Diffusion-curve rendering assumes the boundary conditions describe the intended smooth color behavior. The evidence shows approaches and claimed contributions, but it does not prove broad performance, artist workflow quality, or failure behavior on every messy drawing, noisy scan, or extreme geometric case.

sound-multisensory.problem_shape: This family is about making a designed experience survive contact with the body and the physical world. In ProXeek, the screen can show a virtual object, but the user's hand still meets an ordinary room. The problem is to make that room supply a believable touch target without custom machines or a prebuilt prop. In Mechanical Cloaking of Halftoned Imagery, the object must do two jobs at once: from the outside it should show a target picture made from pores, while mechanically it should behave like one plain material rather than a patterned weak-and-strong patchwork. The shared shape of the problem is cross-sense agreement. A visual design, a touch sensation, and a physical response all have to line up enough that the user or observer accepts the object. The papers are siblings because both refuse to treat appearance as separate from matter. They ask how to choose or design physical structure so it carries a second meaning: a room object can stand in for virtual touch, and a porous material can hide a picture inside a nearly uniform mechanical behavior.
sound-multisensory.naive_failure: A smart beginner would try to solve each sense separately. For virtual reality touch, they might 3D-print a replica, buy a force-feedback device, or let the user see the object without feeling it. That fails because replicas require preparation, active devices are bulky and expensive, and visual-only interaction leaves the hand with no matching evidence. For halftoned mechanical imagery, they might simply punch darker and lighter pore patterns to match a picture. That fails because the same holes that make the image also change how forces travel through the object. A dark region could become softer or directionally biased, so an outside mechanical test would reveal the hidden pattern. In both cases, the simple plan forgets that the body and material do not read labels. They respond to size, position, texture, stiffness, porosity, and direction of force all at once.
sound-multisensory.mathematical_principle: The recurring mathematical idea is constrained matching: choose a physical arrangement that satisfies several kinds of evidence at the same time. In ProXeek, the system starts with virtual objects annotated by designers with emphasized touch qualities. It also receives snapshots of the user's real environment from a commodity headset. The question is not merely which object has the right name. The chosen proxy must plausibly match touch qualities, fit the virtual object's role, and satisfy geometric limits such as where the object is and whether the user can use it. The system scores competing room objects against several goals, then selects viable proxies. In Mechanical Cloaking, the adjustable thing is a parametric porous structure, meaning a family of hole patterns controlled by settings. The structure must visually act like halftoning, where small light and dark marks combine into an image, while its averaged mechanical behavior remains close to uniform and direction-independent. What counts as wrong is concrete: poor visual contrast, a bad match to the target picture, or effective stiffness that changes with direction or location. The tradeoff is expressiveness versus concealment: enough visible variation to draw an image, but not enough mechanical variation to betray it.
sound-multisensory.why_math_matters: The math matters because these are not one-property objects. A room object in ProXeek is useful only through a bundle of relations: it has a shape, a material feel, a place in the room, and a possible correspondence to a virtual object. No single rule such as pick the nearest object can capture that bundle. The matching logic exploits the fact that real environments already contain many possible substitutes, and that language-and-image reasoning can connect descriptions like hardness, texture, and object purpose to visible room evidence. Mechanical Cloaking exploits a different structure: a porous material has two scales. Up close, holes form visible dots that can make a halftone image. From the viewpoint of a larger force test, many holes together can behave like an averaged material. If the pore family is chosen carefully, the visual pattern can vary while the averaged mechanical response stays nearly the same in all directions. In both papers, the math is bookkeeping for hidden coupling: changing what is seen also changes what is felt or how force passes through.
sound-multisensory.paper_family: ProXeek and Mechanical Cloaking look different on the surface, but both are about assigning physical things a second role without breaking their first role. ProXeek keeps the user's room as itself, then asks whether a pillow, cup, table, or other found object can also serve as a virtual touch proxy. Its central move is to compare designer-provided haptic intent with headset-captured room evidence, using multimodal reasoning and a multi-goal scoring process to find candidates that feel more convincing than visual-only interaction or generic printed replicas. Mechanical Cloaking starts with fabricated matter rather than a furnished room. It designs porous structures whose holes form a target image like a printed halftone, while numerical experiments show the structure can remain close to mechanically homogeneous and isotropic, meaning it responds almost like one uniform material and not like a directional pattern. One paper searches existing matter for a perceptual match; the other designs matter so perception and force response can coexist. The common deeper move is to treat perception as a constraint on physical structure, not as a surface decoration added after the real object is chosen.
sound-multisensory.what_changed: The 2026 version of this family seems to push multisensory graphics toward ordinary physical settings. ProXeek does not assume a special haptic lab; it uses commodity headset snapshots and objects already in the user's environment. Mechanical Cloaking does not treat a picture as only ink or pixels; it asks whether the visual image can be embedded into load-bearing porous structure while hiding its mechanical trace. The shift is from adding separate sensory hardware or decorative appearance toward making physical context do more work. These papers also show a stronger concern for competing requirements: touch match versus availability and geometry in ProXeek, visual contrast versus uniform mechanical behavior in Mechanical Cloaking.
sound-multisensory.limits: The evidence is narrow. ProXeek depends on designer annotations, headset snapshots, available room objects, and the reasoning system's ability to infer touch-relevant properties from visual and language evidence. A room with poor substitutes, unsafe layouts, hidden object properties, or unusual virtual interactions could break the match, and the user study does not prove every home or application will work. Mechanical Cloaking depends on the chosen class of porous structures and numerical experiments; the abstract does not prove that any target image, material, scale, or manufacturing process will preserve near-uniform mechanical behavior. Both papers also rely on perception thresholds: the touch proxy or cloaked material only has to be convincing enough under the tested conditions, not physically identical to the thing it represents.

vr-ar-displays.problem_shape: These papers belong together because they all ask how a display can make the eye receive the intended light, not merely show an image on a flat panel. In VR and AR, the display is part of the optical system. It may need to place light at different apparent depths, make a transparent glass sheet reconstruct a full-color 3D image, create bright points floating in a real volume, keep a remote avatar lit like the local room, or preserve visible detail while the display surface changes shape. The shared pressure is that the viewer judges the final light field, color, depth cue, brightness, and motion, while the hardware can only control limited things: laser power, phase patterns, surface grooves, scanning mirrors, LED strips, headset cameras, or a small number of path-traced samples. The family is therefore about translating a desired experience into physical light commands. A paper is not only drawing pixels. It is deciding which pieces of light must be sent, delayed, bent, sampled, colored, or refreshed so the viewer's eye gets a coherent scene.
vr-ar-displays.naive_failure: A smart beginner might treat the display as a normal screen: render a sharp RGB image, send it to the device, and expect the viewer to see the intended scene. That fails because these devices do not simply copy pixel values into the eye. A holographic display must control wave interference, so depth, view change, focus blur, and glossy reflections depend on how light waves combine. A transparent surface-relief hologram must work across colors while staying see-through. A volumetric laser display must put enough bright points in space without exceeding hardware and safety limits. A spinning shape-changing display must keep pixel spacing stable while its surface area expands. A headset avatar system must separate body motion, surface color, shine, and room lighting. Plain image rendering ignores the optical and physical path between command and perception.
vr-ar-displays.mathematical_principle: The recurring mathematical idea is controlled mapping from desired perception to limited device actions. The method starts with a target: a color the viewer should judge as correct, a 3D image reconstructed from glass, a bright volume point, a relightable avatar, a moving afterimage surface, or a hologram with natural depth cues. It then asks what device settings could produce that target after physics gets involved. What is adjusted varies by paper: color coordinates and laser illumination in PAColorHolo, shallow surface patterns and frequency bands in the invisible holographic window, synchronized beam paths in the dual-path volumetric display, angular speed, pole height, strip length, and refresh columns in MorphSkein, or avatar shape, shine, diffuse color, and surrounding light in EgoRelight. What counts as wrong is also concrete: color mismatch, crosstalk between color channels, dim or sparse volume points, lost pixel density, broken shape fidelity, or an avatar that does not match the observed headset view. The tradeoff is accuracy versus device bandwidth and refresh speed. The math measures those errors, then changes the controllable settings while respecting optical, geometric, timing, and hardware limits.
vr-ar-displays.why_math_matters: The math matters because displays exploit regular structure in light and motion. Light waves interfere in predictable ways: if the phase pattern is chosen carefully, the viewer sees a depth cue instead of a flat patch. Different colors travel through diffractive structures differently, so a full-color transparent hologram needs frequency separation, meaning putting different color instructions into different spatial bands so they do not corrupt each other. Laser-excited volume displays need coordinated scanning because brightness and point density come from where beams meet space over time. Persistence of vision, meaning the eye blends fast repeated flashes into a continuous image, lets MorphSkein use spinning LED strips as a surface, but only if the release of rows and columns matches the changing troposkein shape. Headset relighting works because shine changes with view and light while diffuse surface color is more stable. These are not decorative equations. They are the bookkeeping rules that connect a device command to what the eye finally sees.
vr-ar-displays.paper_family: The representative papers are versions of the same deeper move: turn a desired visual experience into a device-specific light plan. PAColorHolo starts from the fact that holographic color is distorted by lasers, spatial light modulators, lens color errors, and camera response, so it learns and controls a color mapping that better matches human judgment. The invisible holographic window works from the opposite physical object: a transparent glass surface must remain transmissive while still reconstructing a full-color 3D image, so it uses shallow sinusoidal relief and spatial-frequency band division rather than three separate color holograms. HoloPathTracer connects display design to light transport by solving ordinary scene light paths and wave propagation together, so phase-only holograms can preserve focus cues and material effects. The dual-path volumetric display uses synchronized lasers, modulators, mirrors, and a varifocal lens to raise brightness and point density in physical space. MorphSkein treats a spinning changing surface as the display, preserving density by releasing rows and rendering extra columns as area grows. EgoRelight is the social VR branch: capture, relight, and integrate a user from a headset view.
vr-ar-displays.what_changed: The 2026 version of this family seems less satisfied with flat-image quality and more concerned with the whole perception pipeline. The evidence emphasizes depth cues, parallax, focus, color fidelity, transparent display surfaces, room-light-visible volumetric graphics, relightable avatars, and shape-changing displays that preserve density. Another change is that hardware and computation are treated as one design problem. PAColorHolo adjusts color and illumination around device distortions. HoloPathTracer joins scene light paths with wave propagation. The invisible window changes the surface profile to improve transmittance. The dual-path display doubles and coordinates optical paths. MorphSkein changes both geometry and refresh behavior. The family is moving from showing images toward controlling physical light delivery.
vr-ar-displays.limits: These papers depend on device assumptions that may not transfer. PAColorHolo needs the display, camera response, lasers, and viewer study conditions to match its color model. The invisible holographic window trades full-color transparency for a reduced viewing angle and depends on manufacturable surface relief. HoloPathTracer reports simulations and prototype validation, but practical holographic displays still face computation and hardware constraints. The dual-path volumetric display uses femtosecond lasers, synchronized optics, an Xe-filled volume, and safety controls. MorphSkein assumes ideal troposkein geometry; wrong angular speed, motor limits, MCU speed, or LED refresh can reduce density and shape fidelity. EgoRelight depends on headset camera views, learned appearance behavior, and recoverable room lighting. The evidence does not prove universal performance across all users, rooms, content, devices, or long deployments.
